title: Ukwa
author: Chioma Adeleke
desc: Seven grams of edible potash to seven hundred grams of breadfruit — exactly one per cent — and the test is whether the seeds melt when pressed.
longDesc: Ukwa is African breadfruit cooked to a porridge and it is notorious for how long it takes. The useful thing this recipe gives you is not a time, because it does not state one, but a tactile test that is better than a clock: the ukwa is done when the seeds melt when pressed. Breadfruit varies by age and dryness, so a timing would mislead. What is precisely given is the alkali — seven grams of edible potash to seven hundred grams of breadfruit, exactly one per cent by weight, which tenderises the seeds. A pressure cooker does it in thirty minutes.
equipment: Large heavy pot, or a pressure cooker
steps: Pick over the breadfruit and wash it well.
Dissolve the 7 g of potash in a little water and sieve it, leaving the sediment behind.
Put the breadfruit in a pot with water to cover and the sieved potash water.
Cook till well done, topping up the water as needed. The ukwa is done when the seeds melt when pressed.
Add the dry fish, the stock cubes, pepper and salt.
Add palm oil, enough to colour it, and cook about 5 minutes.
Add the fresh bitter leaves and simmer till the leaves wilt but are still green.
Serve hot. It thickens considerably as it cools.
chefTips: Seeds melting when pressed is the test. Press one against the side of the pot with a spoon — if it gives way completely, you are there.
Seven grams to seven hundred is one per cent by weight. That is a precise figure from a named source and it is worth weighing rather than guessing.
Sieve the potash water and leave the sediment, as with every other alkali step in this collection.
No total cooking time is given anywhere on the source page, and that is honest rather than careless — breadfruit varies enormously with age and dryness.
A pressure cooker does it in 30 minutes, at pressure setting 1 and heat level 7 on the source's equipment.
Leaves wilted but still green is the finishing cue. Overcooked bitter leaf goes olive and tastes flat.
It gets thicker as it cools. Serve it a little looser than you want to eat it.
commonMistakes: Cooking to a clock instead of to the press test.
Guessing the potash rather than weighing it.
Letting the pot run dry during the long cook.
Judging the final consistency while it is piping hot.
servedWith: On its own, as a porridge
sources: Adapted from 'African Breadfruit (Ukwa)', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 700g African Breadfruit; 2 medium dry fish; 2 small stock cubes; 7g edible potash; Palm oil (enough to colour) — no quantity; 5-6 fresh bitter leaves; Pepper & Salt to taste.
THE ALKALI RATIO: 7 g of potash to 700 g of breadfruit, exactly 1 per cent by weight. This is one of the few precisely weighed alkali figures in any Nigerian source consulted.
TOTAL CONVENTIONAL COOKING TIME IS NOT STATED. The page says cook 'till well done' with water topped up as needed. That gap was specifically searched for and is confirmed rather than filled.
THE DONENESS CUE, verbatim and better than a clock: 'The ukwa is done when the seeds melt when pressed.'
A pressure-cooker time IS given: 30 minutes, at 'pressure setting 1 and heat level 7'.

Other times and cues as printed: palm oil stage 'about 5 minutes'; leaves simmered 'till the leaves wilt but still green'. Headnote: 'African breadfruit is in a food class of its own' and 'Breadfruit Porridge gets thicker as it cools down.' Yield not specified.

A SECOND PAGE on the same site, 'The BEST Way to Cook Ukwa, My Favourite Way Anyway', carries NO quantities for anything, no times and no cues, with its instructions in an embedded video. Its author flags it explicitly as a personal deviation — calling it 'my favourite best way', insisting extra ingredients 'ruin the natural delicious taste of ukwa', preferring 'freshly peeled ukwa' over dry, and describing a personal practice of adding a 'small quantity' of akanwu with pressure cooking. That page is not used for quantities here, but the author-declared preference is recorded.

For the alkali's chemistry and the safety note that belongs beside this recipe — including the fact that 'potash' is the wrong word for it — see NGA120. NOTE that no source consulted discusses kaun in ukwa specifically; the Koleosho condiment article lists its functions as tenderiser, vegetable enhancer, flavour enhancer, emulsifier, preservative and colour additive, and names tough meat, bone, cowpeas, cow-foot and stockfish under tenderising, but not ukwa.
storage: 4 days refrigerated. It sets very firm.
reheating: Low heat with plenty of water to loosen it back to a porridge.
healthBenefits: African breadfruit is high in protein, fibre, iron and potassium.
Very filling for its calorie count.
Bitter leaf is traditionally used for digestion.
culturalNote: Ukwa is a seasonal Igbo dish and a well-loved one, and its reputation rests partly on how much patience it takes. The seed comes from Treculia africana, the African breadfruit tree, and it is sold both fresh and dried — dried takes considerably longer. That the best instruction anyone gives is press a seed and see whether it melts says something true about cooking an ingredient that varies this much.
